title: Knowledge transfer & learning from experience
blurb: Explain why knowledge transfer is vital at transition, how to do it, and how learning from experience drives continuous improvement.
question: A rail signalling upgrade is about to hand over. Only the supplier's lead engineer knows how to clear the most common faults, and she leaves in a month. The team also wants to stop its next project repeating this one's mistakes. Why does knowledge transfer matter here, and what should the project do?

teach.h: Handing over what people know, not just what they built
teach.body: Knowledge transfer is handing over the knowledge needed to operate and support the project's outputs, through documentation, training, shadowing and handover workshops. It also covers learning from experience (lessons learned) and continuous improvement, so the organisation gets better at projects. In plain English: the people who will run the outputs must know how, and the next project should start smarter than this one did.

teach.caption: One direction protects THIS project's benefits; the other improves FUTURE projects.

rows.label: What it is
values: Written down and easy to share

rows.label: Example
values: Knowing which fault alarm to ignore

rows.label: Risk if missed
values: Knowledge walks out of the door

teach.caption: Documents alone rarely transfer tacit knowledge. That's why shadowing and hands-on workshops matter.

head: Method
Best for
Example
rows: BAU engineer works beside the supplier
Walk-through of open issues and risks

teach.body: If BAU can't operate or fix the outputs, adoption stalls and benefits are delayed or lost. Poor transfer leaves the organisation dependent on a few individuals or an expensive supplier, causes avoidable faults and floods the support desk. Good transfer shortens the bedding-in period, protects the business case and lets the project close cleanly. Planning it from the outset means BAU staff can learn alongside the project rather than in a rush at the end.

teach.caption: A lesson is only learned when it is APPLIED. Recording it is just the first step.

rows.label: Linear vs iterative
values: Linear: reviews at gates plus final review

teach.caption: Use both: improve while you deliver, and pass on what you learned. Start each project by reading past lessons.

teach.body: Four weeks before handover, two BAU maintenance engineers shadow the supplier's lead engineer on every fault call. The supplier updates the maintenance manuals and runs a handover workshop covering open defects. During delivery, monthly reviews led to changes such as booking track access earlier. The post-project review, run on a no-blame basis, records lessons in the PMO's library, and the next upgrade's kick-off starts by reviewing them.

teach.text: Recording lessons is not learning them. Options such as 'store lessons in the project file', 'capture lessons only when things go badly' or 'limit lessons to senior managers' are wrong. Lessons must be shared and APPLIED. A review that hunts for blame kills honesty: capture what went well as well as what didn't.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define knowledge transfer: handing over the knowledge needed to operate and support the outputs.
Name methods: documentation, training, shadowing, handover workshops (tacit knowledge needs hands-on methods).
Explain why: BAU can run the outputs, adoption and benefits follow, dependency on individuals falls.
Explain learning from experience: capture, share and apply lessons, at the start, during and at the end.
Link to continuous improvement: feedback loops during delivery improve this project and future ones.
Knowledge transfer: handing over the knowledge BAU needs to operate and support the outputs.
Methods: documentation, training, shadowing, handover workshops; tacit knowledge needs hands-on methods.
Learning from experience: lessons captured, shared and applied, not just stored.
Continuous improvement happens during delivery; the post-project review helps future projects.
Good transfer protects benefits and reduces dependency on key individuals or suppliers.

summary: You can now explain why knowledge transfer is vital to transition and choose methods that suit explicit and tacit knowledge. You can also explain how lessons learned and continuous improvement help both this project and future ones.

A.q: What is the main purpose of knowledge transfer during transition?
options: To return the project budget to the finance team
To log the change requests raised during delivery
To set the success criteria for the next project
To give BAU what it needs to run the outputs
A.why: Knowledge transfer equips BAU with the knowledge needed to operate and support the outputs, so benefits can be realised.

whyNot.0: Returning unused budget is part of financial close-down.
whyNot.1: Change requests are logged throughout, in the change log.
whyNot.2: The next project sets its own success criteria.

A.q: Which method is BEST for transferring tacit knowledge?
options: Emailing out the user manual
Shadowing an expert engineer
Filing all the test records
Publishing the full schedule
A.why: Tacit knowledge lives in people's experience, so it transfers best through hands-on methods like shadowing.

whyNot.0: Manuals carry explicit knowledge; tacit know-how rarely makes it onto the page.
whyNot.2: Test records are explicit documents and don't pass on experience.
whyNot.3: A schedule shows timing, not operating know-how.

A.q: A lessons log is completed at closure but never read again. What is the MAIN problem?
options: The log breaches data protection rules
The sponsor must re-approve the case
The lessons won't improve future work
The project can't be formally closed
A.why: Lessons only add value when they are shared and applied; an unread log changes nothing.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests a data protection breach.
whyNot.1: The business case isn't affected by an unread lessons log.
whyNot.3: Closure can still happen; the loss is to future projects.

B.q: How does continuous improvement differ from a post-project review?
options: It happens during delivery, not after
It is only used on linear projects
It removes the need to capture lessons
It is carried out by external auditors
B.why: Continuous improvement adjusts ways of working during delivery; a post-project review looks back after completion to help future projects.

whyNot.1: It is used in both life cycles, and is built into iterative retrospectives.
whyNot.2: Lessons are still captured; continuous improvement acts on them sooner.
whyNot.3: It is led by the team and project manager, not external auditors.

B.q:
Which TWO actions make lessons learned effective?
1) Sharing them across the organisation
2) Recording only major failures
3) Applying them on new projects
4) Limiting them to the core team
options: 1 and 4
2 and 3
2 and 4
1 and 3
B.why: Lessons are effective when they are shared widely and applied to new work.

whyNot.0: Sharing is good, but limiting lessons to the core team stops them spreading.
whyNot.1: Applying is good, but recording only failures misses what worked.
whyNot.2: Both narrow the value of lessons rather than increasing it.

B.q: At the start of a new project, a project manager reviews lessons from similar past projects. Why?
options: To find out who caused past failures
To copy the old schedule unchanged
To avoid repeating known mistakes
To replace the need for risk management
B.why: Applying past lessons at the start is how organisations avoid repeating mistakes and reuse what worked.

whyNot.0: Lessons are about learning, not blame.
whyNot.1: Every project is unique; lessons inform the plan rather than replace it.
whyNot.3: Lessons feed risk identification; they don't replace risk management.

C.q: A supplier built a hospital's new pharmacy system. At handover, only the supplier's lead developer knows how to fix common faults, and she leaves next month. What is the BEST action?
options: Ask her to email a short list of tips
Arrange shadowing and fault workshops
Delay go-live until a new supplier is found
Accept the risk and close the project now
C.why: Her knowledge is tacit, so BAU staff should shadow her and work through real faults in workshops before she leaves.

whyNot.0: A short email won't capture tacit know-how.
whyNot.2: Changing supplier doesn't transfer the knowledge and delays benefits.
whyNot.3: Closing with that gap leaves BAU unable to support the system.

C.q: A team's retrospectives keep surfacing the same problem, but nothing changes. What is MISSING?
options: Turning feedback into action
Collecting more feedback
Holding fewer retrospectives
Escalating it to the board
C.why: Continuous improvement needs feedback to be converted into changes; otherwise problems recur.

whyNot.1: They already have feedback; the gap is acting on it.
whyNot.2: Fewer retrospectives would mean less learning, not more.
whyNot.3: Escalation may help with blockers, but the core gap is acting on feedback.

C.q: Which is NOT a benefit of good knowledge transfer?
options: A smoother handover with fewer support calls
Benefits realised sooner after go-live
Less dependency on key individuals
No need for any support period at all
C.why: Good transfer shortens bedding-in, but an agreed support period is still a normal transition requirement.

whyNot.0: Well-prepared BAU staff raise fewer support calls.
whyNot.1: When BAU can run the outputs, adoption and benefits come sooner.
whyNot.2: Spreading knowledge reduces reliance on a few people.

reteach.title: Handing over your café while you're away
reteach.question: You run a busy café and are going on six months' leave. A new manager takes over. How do you make sure she can run it, and how do you both make it better?

blocks.body: You hand over the recipe book, supplier list and opening checklist: that's explicit knowledge. But knowing that the coffee machine needs a tap when it sulks, or which regular wants oat milk without asking, is tacit. For that she shadows you through a busy Saturday. You also share your notebook of what went wrong last summer, and agree to try one small improvement each week and keep what works.

blocks.text: Leaving the notebook in a drawer means the same mistakes happen again. Lessons count only when they are applied.

explain.body: BAU needs to operate, maintain and support the outputs. Hand over documentation, train users and support staff, and use handover workshops to walk through open issues.

test.q: Which item would usually be handed to the BAU support team at transition?
options: The tender evaluation scoresheets
The team's annual leave calendar
Operating and maintenance manuals
The sponsor's appraisal notes
test.why: Operating and maintenance manuals are the explicit knowledge BAU needs to run and support the outputs.

whyNot.0: Tender scores belong to procurement records.
whyNot.1: The team's leave calendar is irrelevant to BAU support.
whyNot.3: Appraisal notes are confidential HR records.

explain.body: Explicit knowledge can be written down. Tacit knowledge is built from experience and lives in people's heads, so it transfers through shadowing, coaching and practice.

test.q: Knowledge held in people's heads and gained through experience is called…
options: explicit knowledge
tacit knowledge
configuration data
baseline information
test.why: Tacit knowledge is experience-based and hard to write down.

whyNot.0: Explicit knowledge is written and easily shared.
whyNot.2: Configuration data records versions and status of items.
whyNot.3: Baseline information is the agreed reference for plans.

explain.body: Review past lessons at the start, capture lessons during the project, and hold a no-blame post-project review at the end. Then share lessons widely and apply them.

test.q: What makes a post-project review MOST likely to produce honest lessons?
options: A no-blame look at what worked and what didn't
Limiting attendance to senior managers only
Focusing only on the things that went wrong
Holding it a year after the team has disbanded
test.why: A balanced, no-blame review encourages people to share openly, including successes worth repeating.

whyNot.1: Excluding the team loses most of the insight.
whyNot.2: Only covering failures damages morale and misses good practice.
whyNot.3: A year later, memories have faded and people have moved on.

explain.body: Feedback loops during delivery (reviews, retrospectives, user feedback) lead to small, regular changes in how the team works, improving the current project, not just the next one.

test.q: Which practice BEST shows continuous improvement during an iterative project?
options: One review at the very end of the project
Fixing the process and refusing all change
Keeping all lessons private to the team
Retrospectives that shape the next time box
test.why: Retrospectives that lead to changes in the next time box are continuous improvement in action.

whyNot.0: A single end review helps future projects, not this one.
whyNot.1: Refusing change is the opposite of improvement.
whyNot.2: Keeping lessons private stops organisational learning.
